extracted.intended_audience: labor lawyers, employers, unions, NLRB stakeholders, and rulemaking commenters/participants
extracted.subtask_description: Agency preamble/response setting standards and explaining legal and evidentiary principles governing the NLRB's joint-employer definition under the NLRA, and addressing public comments on the proposed rule. Intended to guide adjudicators, practitioners, and stakeholders about how the Board will interpret and apply the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker disqualification standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual should be disqualified from rulemaking only when there has been a clear and convincing showing that the official 'has an unalterably closed mind on matters critical to the disposition of the proceeding.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard (citing Air Transportation Ass'n of America v. NMB and C & W Fish Co. v. Fox) requires more than general or speculative suggestions of conflict; commenters' speculative claims regarding Members Wilcox and Prouty were found insufficient under the 'clear and convincing' test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Executive Order 13989 (Ethics Pledge) to rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ethics Pledge applies to 'particular matter[s] involving specific parties that is directly and substantially related to' a former employer or client; general rulemaking that is not such a particular matter does not trigger disqualification under the Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an argument about appearance of conflict is rooted in the Ethics Pledge, the Board treats the pledge as inapplicable unless the rulemaking constitutes a particular matter involving specific parties directly and substantially related to the official's former employers/clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for asserting joint-employer status
rubrics_metrics.description: A party asserting joint-employer status must demonstrate that an entity is a joint employer by a 'preponderance of the evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board rejects commenters' suggestion that the proposed rule should impose an express 'substantial evidence' requirement; the preponderance standard governs allocation of proof when claiming joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the 2020 rule's 'actual-exercise' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 rule's actual-exercise requirement is impermissible under the Act as contrary to common-law agency principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the Board must follow common-law agency principles in determining employer/employee status, the common law does not dictate every detail of the final rule; the Board's final rule reflects policy choices within common-law bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common-law agency (master-servant) principles to define 'employee'
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress uses the term 'employee' without clearly defining it, courts assume Congress intended the conventional master-servant relationship as understood by common-law agency doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Town & Country Electric; Clackamas; Darden; Community for Creative Non-Violence; Kelley; United Insurance) supports grounding statutory analysis in common-law agency concepts (master/servant terminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of workplace health and safety as an essential term/condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Workplace health and safety should be treated as an essential term or condition of employment; consideration of COVID-19 pandemic impacts on health and safety is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board relied on stakeholder input and real-world developments (including pandemic-related concerns) to include health and safety among essential terms and conditions. The agency found these considerations sufficient to reject arguments that inclusion was arbitrary or capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of an exhaustive list of 'essential terms and conditions' as a limiting principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is modified to provide for an exhaustive list of essential terms and conditions of employment, which serves as a limiting principle on joint-employer scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing an exhaustive list was a policy choice intended to provide a new limiting principle not present in prior joint-employer doctrine and to help justify promulgating a new rule rather than merely rescinding the 2020 rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency authority to promulgate joint-employer definition by rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has authority to 'carry out' provisions of the Act and to define 'joint employer' through rulemaking; Supreme Court precedent endorses the Board's use of rulemaking as a policymaking tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board rejects nondelegation challenges claiming Sec. 6 lacks clear authority; courts have repeatedly endorsed the Board's rulemaking use, including on bargaining obligations (e.g., American Hospital Assn. v. NLRB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation to NLRA (not other statutes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule solely relates to the definition of 'joint employer' under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board explicitly confirms the rule does not purport to define joint-employer status under other statutes; this addresses commenter concerns about cross-statutory application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a definite and readily available standard to avoid vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: A new rule advantageously provides a definite and readily available standard, reducing vagueness-based compliance burdens on businesses (e.g., need to retain counsel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters argued vagueness would increase legal costs for small businesses; the Board finds that adopting a definite standard (as opposed to simply rescinding the 2020 rule) helps address those concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reliance interests and effective date timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency should consider reliance interests and may delay or phase in effective dates; the effective date of the final rule will await the culmination of Congressional review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asserted businesses structured operations in reliance on prior Board law; the Board notes Congressional review can affect the effective date and acknowledges reliance concerns in responding to requests to delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of government-mandated multifirm bargaining concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not mandate multiemployer or multifirm bargaining; businesses remain free to structure their operations as they wish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters likened the proposed rule to government-mandated multiemployer bargaining; the Board rejects that characterization and clarifies the rule imposes no bargaining mandate across multiple firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-employer test is distinct (four-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-employer analysis is a distinct inquiry from joint-employer status and traditionally uses a four-factor test considering: interrelation of operations, common management, centralized control of labor relations, and common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board cites Radio & Television Broadcast Technicians Local Union 1264 v. Broadcast Service of Mobile and explains that single-employer tests remain separate from joint-employer inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical input and stakeholder experience in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may rely on empirical arguments, economic analyses, and stakeholders' experiences when considering the effects of a rule (e.g., EPI analysis and BLS CWS underestimation concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency discusses and gives weight to empirical submissions (including revised estimates and critiques of survey undercounts) in assessing the rule's anticipated effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to evidentiary and arbitrary-capricious challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenters assert that aspects of the proposed rule are unsupported (and thus arbitrary and capricious), the agency must show it considered relevant evidence and reasoned responses — e.g., stakeholder input supporting health and safety inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board explains why it views commenters' objections as unpersuasive by pointing to the record of stakeholder input, legal analysis, and the policy goals in Sec. 1 of the Act to encourage collective bargaining.
